strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: editing images to evoke a target emotion using only an image and an emotion label. The qualitative examples demonstrate changes beyond global color or style transfer.

EmoPair offers a potentially valuable paired resource for emotional image editing, combining 331,595 automatically labeled existing pairs with 6,949 purpose-generated pairs. The underlying datasets and pretrained methods are attributed.

Evaluation includes 504 source images balanced across eight emotions, randomized human comparisons, and a smaller laboratory study. The reported 56% overall online preference provides initial evidence of perceptual benefits beyond classifier scores.

The manuscript provides informative visualizations, explicitly discusses semantic drift and facial-detail failures, and acknowledges potential misuse. Informed consent, institutional ethics approval, and participant compensation are reported.
weaknesses: The automated evaluation is strongly coupled to the method’s optimization. The same predictor P labels and filters training data, selects outputs through up to 20 inference iterations, and computes EMR/ESR. Table 1 shows EMR dropping from 50.20% to 5.06% without this selection mechanism. Consequently, the results do not isolate improvements from the learned editor versus optimization against the evaluator. Baselines should receive comparable sampling budgets and critic-based selection, with independent evaluation and human ablations.

The mathematical specification contains consequential ambiguities. Section 3.2 defines z = E(Is) and noises this source latent for the denoising objective, without introducing the paired target-image latent. As written, this supervises source reconstruction rather than the desired edit. Also, under conventional KL argument ordering, ESR’s KL(eg, eoh) is infinite for a softmax distribution against a one-hot target. These could be notation errors, but the implemented training objective and KL ordering or smoothing must be specified.

The architectural novelty and reasoning claims are insufficiently established. The image and emotion conditioning largely adapt the existing InstructPix2Pix framework. Since e = tau(y) depends only on the emotion label, the alignment loss regularizes a shared class embedding; it does not by itself demonstrate source-specific, human-like reasoning. A same-data, emotion-conditioned InstructPix2Pix baseline is needed. Single-word prompts weaken several comparisons, and the directly related Affective Image Filter [30] is discussed but not evaluated.

The human results do not establish the claimed consistent superiority. Online preferences over NST, CLIP-Styler, and LMS are only 53%, 52%, and 54%, respectively; preference over LMS is 49% in the laboratory study (Fig. S6). No confidence intervals or statistical analysis accounting for repeated participants and images are provided. Only 27% of online participants pass screening, making sensitivity to exclusions relevant. Trial accounting also needs correction: 417 participants × 100 trials is 41,700, not 417,000, and the supplement reports 11,400 trials after screening.

Dataset quality is not adequately validated. Approximately 98% of EmoPair consists of existing pairs labeled by a predictor with 73% accuracy on EmoSet; this does not establish annotation accuracy on synthetic editing pairs. The confidence filtering for EPGS likewise provides no independent human validation. A sampled audit of emotion transitions and content preservation, class/transition statistics, and EPAS-versus-EPGS ablations would substantiate the dataset contribution.

The central content-preservation claim receives limited support. ENRD and ESS measure pixel and edge differences, not semantic preservation, and the human study evaluates emotional preference without jointly assessing fidelity. Substantial content replacement appears in the examples and acknowledged failures. Furthermore, contrary to Section 5.1, both ablations have lower, better ENRD and ESS than the full model, revealing an emotion-versus-fidelity tradeoff. Within-valence editing and neutral-image generalization are supported only by a few qualitative examples.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the promised release. The manuscript and supplement omit learning rate, batch size, training duration, emotion-encoder dimensions, and important inference settings. Runtime and average iteration counts are also absent, preventing assessment of the practical cost of repeated generation.
